papers.title: An apparently de novo UBE3A missense variant p.(Tyr777Cys) in the HECT domain in a child with an atypical early childhood phenotype suggestive of Angelman syndrome: a case report and focused literature review.
papers.abstract: Angelman syndrome (AS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with loss of maternal UBE3A function in neurons. Interpreting rare UBE3A missense variants can be challenging, particularly when parental origin and functional effects have not been established. We report a 30-month-old Chinese boy with global developmental delay, motor impairment, and severe expressive language impairment, without clinically observed seizures during the available follow-up. Genetic evaluation, including trio whole-exome sequencing and proband whole-genome sequencing, identified an apparently de novo heterozygous UBE3A missense variant, NM_130839.5:c.2330A>G, p. (Tyr777Cys), within the homologous to the E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT) domain. Copy-number analysis did not identify a large deletion involving 15q11.2-q13. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed paroxysmal high-amplitude 2-3 Hz spike-slow and sharp-slow complexes, and the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) report suggested delayed white-matter myelination. The variant was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in the laboratory report and remained a VUS following reassessment using the UBE3A-specific ClinGen Variant Curation Expert Panel (VCEP) specifications. Its maternal or paternal allelic origin remains undetermined, and its functional effects have not been experimentally assessed. This report documents the rare, apparently de novo UBE3A HECT-domain variant p. (Tyr777Cys), together with detailed early developmental and electrophysiological findings. Substantial motor and expressive language impairment accompanied by EEG abnormalities suggestive of AS, despite no clinically observed seizures by 30 months, highlights the importance of considering AS during the evaluation of unexplained developmental delay. Integrated clinical assessment, EEG, and family-based genetic testing help identify candidate variants and guide further investigation. Although p. (Tyr777Cys) remains a VUS, the documented phenotype provides a reference for future case comparisons, parent-of-origin studies, and functional investigations.

papers.title: JAK Inhibition in Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome: A Case Series from Sydney Children's Hospital.
papers.abstract: Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) is a subcategory of New-Onset Refractory Status Epilepticus (NORSE) occurring in previously healthy individuals following a mild febrile illness. FIRES is a challenging paediatric condition with a mortality of 12% and permanent neurocognitive deficits in up to 90% of survivors. Pathogenesis appears to involve innate immune dysregulation, and first-line immunotherapy (intravenous immunoglobulin [IVIG], corticosteroids) is ineffective in most cases. A number of second-line cytokine-directed therapies have been trialled in individual case reports and short case series, but with similarly unencouraging outcomes. We describe three paediatric patients managed at Sydney Children's Hospital between 2024 and 2026 in whom baricitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, was incorporated into the immunotherapy regimen for FIRES. Patient 1 was a 13-year-old girl diagnosed with FIRES with refractory status epilepticus. After 2 months of uncontrolled seizures with profound functional decline and brain atrophy, baricitinib was added to her treatment regimen. While she eventually succumbed to her illness, the introduction of JAK inhibition was accompanied by electroencephalogram (EEG) normalisation within two weeks. Patient 2, a 15-year-old girl, presented following a post-appendicectomy febrile illness. She developed refractory status epilepticus with negative autoimmune and paraneoplastic workup and markedly elevated neopterin (347 nmol/L; normal range [NR] = 0 - 30). Treatment with IVIG, methylprednisolone, and plasma exchange (PLEX) followed by baricitinib and anakinra achieved seizure control over a period of weeks. Intermittent focal seizures and encephalopathic EEG changes persist, but with return to premorbid function and return to school. Patient 3 is a 16-year-old girl who presented in March 2026 with febrile encephalopathy and escalating seizures. Following intubation, multi-agent antiepileptic therapy, and immunosuppression, including baricitinib, anakinra, and IVIG, she was extubated after 2 weeks with subsequent functional recovery, returning to school with mild residual cognitive and emotional changes. This case series adds to the limited evidence supporting early and aggressive JAK inhibition in paediatric FIRES. The addition of baricitinib appears to offer clinically meaningful seizure reduction and EEG improvement when used alongside cytokine-directed therapy.

papers.title: Emergence of ANTI-GAD65 Autoimmunity in Longstanding Drug-Resistant Temporal Lobe Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 autoantibodies (anti-GAD65 Abs) are associated with a spectrum of neurological syndromes, including chronic temporal lobe epilepsy. Although immunosuppressive therapy is generally considered less effective in long-standing anti-GAD65-associated epilepsy, emerging evidence suggests that selected patients may derive a meaningful benefit. In 2015, the patient re-presented with altered mental state and increased seizure frequency, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing confirming herpes simplex virus encephalitis. Serum anti-GAD65 Ab testing was negative. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left temporal encephalomalacia. The persistent burden of refractory focal seizures to anti-epileptic therapy in the subsequent years led to the recent consideration of epilepsy surgery. Detection of high-titre serum anti-GAD65 Abs during the workup raised concerns for a diagnosis of autoimmune epilepsy, with anti-GAD65 Abs also detected in CSF. Pre-treatment video electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrated significant seizure burden from the right temporal region with 68 focal seizures in the first 44 hours of evaluation. Rituximab induction was then implemented, along with mycophenolate mofetil and a weaning dose of oral prednisolone. A 24-hour EEG was repeated, which demonstrated one single brief subclinical seizure, representing a marked reduction in seizure burden. Ongoing clinical and electrophysiological follow-up is underway. This case adds to the limited evidence supporting intensive immunosuppressive treatment in selected patients with anti-GAD65-associated chronic epilepsy. It further highlights the potential value of repeat anti-GAD65 Abs testing in patients with longstanding drug-resistant epilepsy with clinical suspicion for autoimmune temporal lobe epilepsy.
